title: Drug Classifications, Generic and Brand Names

sections.learningObjectives:
- Categorize common drug classifications by their therapeutic effect.
- Distinguish between generic (nonproprietary) and brand (trade) drug names.
- Explain why generic names are used in medication documentation.
- Recognize common drug classes, including by familiar generic-name suffixes.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The generic name is like a person's legal, real name: it stays the same no matter who is talking about the medicine or which company made it.

### Question 2

A brand name is like a company's own label or logo for a product; the company owns it and puts a trademark on it.

### Question 3

Using the medicine's real, shared name means that no matter which company made the pill, everyone knows exactly what drug we are talking about.

### Question 4

It is like writing a common noun such as 'dog' in small letters but a proper name such as 'Rex' with a capital letter, so you can tell them apart quickly.

### Question 5

It is like the same ingredient being put into several different boxes with different store labels; the ingredient inside is still the same.

### Question 6

If two boxes have the same key ingredient in the same amount, they do the same job, just like two recipes with the same ingredients turn out the same.

### Question 7

Ibuprofen is the real name of the medicine, while Advil and Motrin are the company 'nicknames' for it.

### Question 8

Tylenol is the company's own label name, while acetaminophen is the medicine's real name.

### Question 9

Giving the medicine one shared real name means every doctor and nurse is talking about the same thing, no matter where they work.

### Question 10

A brand name is like a company's owned logo for its product, marked with a capital letter.

### Question 11

An analgesic is a 'pain reliever,' like a medicine that turns down the volume on pain signals.

### Question 12

An antibiotic is a 'bacteria fighter'; it only works on germs called bacteria.

### Question 13

An antipyretic is a 'fever reducer,' helping bring a high temperature back down.

### Question 14

An antihypertensive helps lower high blood pressure, like turning down pressure in a hose.

### Question 15

An anticoagulant is a 'blood thinner'; it makes it harder for dangerous clots to form.

### Question 16

An antihistamine calms the body's overreaction to things like pollen, easing sneezes and itches.

### Question 17

A bronchodilator is an 'airway opener,' like widening a straw so air flows through more easily.

### Question 18

A diuretic is a 'water pill'; it helps the body get rid of extra fluid through urine.

### Question 19

An antidiabetic helps bring high blood sugar back down, like a helper that keeps sugar levels from getting too high.

### Question 20

An antidepressant is a medicine that helps lift a person's mood when they have depression.

### Question 21

NSAIDs are 'swelling calmers' that ease pain and puffiness without being steroids.

### Question 22

An antacid is like a splash of water on an acid spill, calming the burning in the stomach.

### Question 23

An antiemetic is a 'no more throwing up' helper that calms nausea.

### Question 24

An antifungal is a 'fungus fighter' that clears up infections like yeast.

### Question 25

An antiviral is a 'virus fighter'; it only works against germs called viruses.

### Question 26

Corticosteroids are strong 'inflammation calmers' that help quiet swelling and overreaction in the body.

### Question 27

Beta-blockers are like a brake pedal that helps slow the heart and lower blood pressure.

### Question 28

ACE inhibitors help blood vessels relax and widen, like opening a garden hose so water flows with less pressure.

### Question 29

Statins are 'cholesterol lowerers' that help keep arteries from getting clogged.

### Question 30

Opioids are strong pain medicines that must be watched very carefully because they can be misused.

### Question 31

Benzodiazepines are calming medicines that must be handled carefully because they can be habit-forming.

### Question 32

A muscle relaxant is like a gentle stretch in a pill that helps tight muscles loosen up.

### Question 33

A laxative helps a person go to the bathroom when they are constipated.

### Question 34

A vaccine is like a practice drill for the body's defense team so it is ready if the real germ ever shows up.

### Question 35

A PPI turns down the stomach's acid-making machine, while an antacid just cleans up acid that is already there.

### Question 36

The -olol ending is a clue, like a name tag, telling us the medicine belongs to the beta-blocker family.

### Question 37

The -pril ending is a clue that the medicine belongs to the ACE inhibitor family.

### Question 38

The -statin ending is a clue that the medicine is a cholesterol lowerer.

### Question 39

The -cillin ending is a clue that the medicine is an antibiotic in the penicillin family.

### Question 40

The -prazole ending is a clue that the medicine turns down stomach acid production.

### Question 41

The -sartan ending is a clue for the ARB family, another group of blood-pressure medicines.

### Question 42

The -pam and -lam endings are clues that a medicine is a calming, tightly controlled drug that needs careful record-keeping.

### Question 43

The -dipine ending is a clue for the calcium channel blocker family of blood-pressure medicines.

### Question 44

The -floxacin ending is a clue for one family of antibiotics.

### Question 45

The -cycline ending is a clue for the tetracycline family of antibiotics.

### Question 46

An anticonvulsant helps calm the brain's electrical storms that cause seizures.

### Question 47

Write down the medicine's real name so everyone on the team knows exactly what drug it is.

### Question 48

When two medicine names look alike, write the whole name carefully so nobody mixes them up.

### Question 49

Listing everything is like showing all the puzzle pieces so the doctor can see the whole picture.

### Question 50

Advil's real name is ibuprofen; that is the ingredient inside the box.

### Question 51

When unsure about a medicine, check the reference book and ask an expert; never guess.

### Question 52

Write the allergy in big, clear letters so no one gives that medicine by mistake.

### Question 53

The label has to show the medicine's real name too, not just the brand name.

### Question 54

Making part of the name BIG helps people see the difference between two confusingly similar medicine names.

### Question 55

A class is a family, and metoprolol is one named member of the beta-blocker family.

### Question 56

An antitussive turns down the cough reflex, while an expectorant helps loosen mucus.

### Question 57

A decongestant is a 'nose unstuffer' that opens up a blocked nose.

### Question 58

An antidiarrheal helps slow down watery stools.

### Question 59

Insulin is a helper hormone that lowers high blood sugar.

### Question 60

Nitrates open up blood vessels to ease the heart's workload and relieve chest pain.

### Question 61

Levothyroxine gives back the thyroid hormone the body is missing.

### Question 62

SSRIs help balance a brain chemical called serotonin, which can lift mood.

### Question 63

Antipsychotics help with conditions where a person loses touch with reality.

### Question 64

Birth control pills use hormones to prevent pregnancy.

### Question 65

Three different endings, -pril, -olol, and -sartan, point to three different families of blood-pressure medicines.

### Question 66

Even medicines from the store shelf count and can mix badly with other medicines.

### Question 67

Same real name equals same ingredient, just a different label on the box.

### Question 68

The real name stays the same, but companies can put many different labels on the same medicine over the years.

### Question 69

Choosing which medicine to take is the doctor's and pharmacist's job; the assistant points the patient to the right expert.

### Question 70

Many antibiotics end in -mycin, which is a clue they are germ fighters.

### Question 71

Antibiotics only fight bacteria, and colds come from viruses, so antibiotics would not help.

### Question 72

Both calm swelling, but corticosteroids are the strong 'steroid' family and NSAIDs are the nonsteroid family.

### Question 73

Water pills flush out extra fluid, and important body salts can go with it, so the doctor checks those salts.

### Question 74

Warfarin makes blood slower to clot, so it is extra important for the team to know a patient takes it.

### Question 75

Ibuprofen calms swelling too, while acetaminophen mostly eases pain and fever.

### Question 76

Metformin is a medicine that helps lower high blood sugar.

### Question 77

Levothyroxine is the real name, and Synthroid is the brand label.

### Question 78

Albuterol is the real name, and Ventolin and ProAir are just different brand labels for it.

### Question 79

Amoxicillin is an antibiotic in the penicillin family.

### Question 80

Lisinopril is the real name, Zestril and Prinivil are brand labels, and 'ACE inhibitor' is the family it belongs to.

### Question 81

Atorvastatin is the real name, and Lipitor is the brand label.

### Question 82

Benadryl's real name is diphenhydramine, an allergy medicine.

### Question 83

Furosemide, also called Lasix, is a water pill that helps the body get rid of extra fluid.

### Question 84

Oxycodone is a strong, tightly controlled pain medicine, so it gets careful, exact record-keeping.

### Question 85

Tightly controlled medicines need careful, honest records and following the rules.
